(2) `if (cond) v = 5 else v = 9;` is a two-way branch on the already-declared boolean `cond` assigning 5 in the true arm and 9 in the false arm. (3) `return v;` reads `v` after the branch and returns it. F-2: language only. F-3: builds and runs under the frozen recipe and prints 5 for cond = true. F-4/F-6: clean. HONEST DISCLOSURE, recorded because it is a real surface fact and costs Zig one token: Zig does NOT permit `var v: i32;`. The initializer token is mandatory; what Zig provides is a token that means 'uninitialized', not the ability to omit the initializer. R10 FORM SELECTION: braceless arms `if (cond) v = 5 else v = 9;` = 12 tokens (SELECTED); braced arms `if (cond) { v = 5; } else { v = 9; }` = 17 tokens. Both satisfy R1-R3, both are accepted by `zig fmt` unchanged, and both are ordinary Zig; fewest tokens wins. The expression form `v = if (cond) 5 else 9;` would be 10 tokens but was REJECTED under R1: sub-requirement (2) requires the branch to ASSIGN in each arm, and the expression form assigns once outside the arms.

(1) `put` is a one-parameter function taking `out: *i32` - writable access to a caller-owned signed 32-bit integer - whose body is exactly the one assignment `out.* = 12;`. (2) `var cell: i32 = 3;` is a mutable caller local of the same integer type. (3) `put(&cell);` calls it using the explicit form Zig REQUIRES for this purpose: the `&` at the call site is mandatory, because a bare `put(cell)` cannot bind an `i32` to a `*i32` parameter, and the `*i32` at the parameter is mandatory, because Zig function parameters are immutable and no other mechanism lets a callee write a caller's local. The alternative - `fn put` at container scope with the caller's statements in a function - is equally idiomatic Zig and needs no wrapper, but would split the fragment in two. Per the frozen rubric's own note under P-e, a scaffold required by the harness rather than by the language is NOT a PARTIAL, so this is FULL; the wrapper's tokens are counted in full against Zig rather than excused, which is the conservative direction. Referring to a declaration of a struct type expression without calling it yields the function as a value of type `*const fn(...) ...`.

A generic type is produced by calling a function at compile time, and a decl literal `.empty` is resolved against the annotated type.
`for` loop over a slice with a capture `|e|`.
A `for` capture is by value and immutable unless a pointer capture `|*e|` is written, so a loop cannot write back into the sequence without saying so.
`try` expression.
`try` requires the enclosing function's return type to be an error union.
Method-call syntax `a.b(c)`, which passes `a` as the first parameter.
`std.ArrayList(T).append(allocator, item)` appends one element at the end and may allocate through the allocator passed at that call.
`std.ArrayList(T).append` returns `Allocator.Error!void`, so failure is signalled as an error value rather than an exception.
`std.ArrayList(T).items` is the slice of the elements currently stored, in insertion order.

Indexing a slice (runtime length) is bounds-checked and panics in Debug and ReleaseSafe, and is undetected illegal behaviour in ReleaseFast and ReleaseSmall; indexing an array or a `*[N]T` with a comptime-known index is checked at compile time instead.
